newsitem.title: USA: GM Pontiac strike talks move slowly, UAW says.
newsitem.headline: GM Pontiac strike talks move slowly, UAW says.

text.p: Negotiations to resolve General Motors Corp.'s truck plant strike in Pontiac, Mich., resumed Thursday but quickly bogged down to the same slow pace of two other auto industry labor disputes, union officials said.

"GM is dragging their feet," said Roger Coats, financial secretary of United Auto Workers Local 594. "The main issue is manpower, and they're talking about drinking fountains and other Mickey Mouse stuff."
Coats said at the current pace, he believes the strike may not be settled for more than two weeks. Talks recessed late Thursday afternoon and were scheduled to resume Friday morning.

About 5,850 workers struck the Pontiac East plant and related facilities Wednesday over demands that GM hire about 600 new employees to ease workloads and replace jobs lost to retirements. The plant makes GM's popular Chevrolet and GMC full-size extended cab pickups.
Negotiations also continued to move slowly in strikes at GM's Oklahoma City car plants and at Chrysler Corp.'s Mound Road engine plant in Detroit.

Including strikers, the three walkouts have idled 33,862 GM and Chrysler workers in the United States, Canada and Mexico, including 9,920 at GM and 23,942 at Chrysler. Some suppliers also have sent workers home.
The 20-day Oklahoma City strike has cut off the only source for GM's new Oldsmobile Cutlass sedan and the primary source for the new Chevrolet Malibu.

The 15-day Chrysler engine strike has forced the automaker to halt production of its Jeep Grand Cherokee sport utility vehicles in Detroit, its large vans in Windsor, Ontario, and its Dodge Ram and Dakota pickup trucks in Warren, Mich., Fenton, Mo., and Lago Alberto and Saltillo, Mexico.

Chrysler officials, who have not met face-to-face with UAW bargainers since the walkout began, continued to talk only over the telephone with them, while normal negotiations continued in Oklahoma City on Thursday.

In Pontiac, the UAW's Coats said GM was in no hurry to settle the strike because its dealers had a 65-day supply of Chevrolet C/K pickups and a 71-day supply of GMC Sierra pickups. Automakers consider a 60- to 65-day supply to be ideal.
GM also disclosed Thursday that it has scheduled overtime production next week at its two other full-size pickup truck plants, in Oshawa, Ontario, and Fort Wayne, Ind.
GM spokesman Thomas Beaman said GM doesn't want a long strike, but it wants an agreement that allows it to become competitive.
"We continue to want to work with them to get an agreement as soon as possible. We want to get back to building trucks."
A strike last month at GM's Fort Wayne, Ind., truck plant went about two weeks before GM settled it by agreeing to add 276 additional workers to the plant's payroll.
